title: Certifying Almost all Quantum States with Few Single-Qubit Measurements
authors: Hsin-Yuan Huang (Google Quantum AI, USA; California Institute of Technology, USA; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA), John Preskill (California Institute of Technology, USA; AWS Center for Quantum Computing, USA), Mehdi Soleimanifar (California Institute of Technology, USA)
abstract: A fundamental challenge in quantum information science is certifying that an $n$-qubit state $\rho$ prepared in the lab closely matches a target state $\ket{\psi}$. Previous approaches to this problem often require deep quantum circuits, exponentially many single-qubit measurements, or are limited to specific state families. In this work, we introduce a new method that leverages a connection between state certification and the mixing time of a random walk, allowing almost all $n$-qubit target states, including those with exponential circuit complexity, to be certified with only $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ single-qubit measurements. Our protocol is broadly compatible with various experimental platforms and has applications in benchmarking quantum systems, optimizing quantum circuits, and efficiently learning and verifying representations of quantum states---such as neural networks and tensor networks---using only single-qubit measurements. Moreover, these verified representations enable the efficient prediction of highly non-local properties of $\rho$ that would otherwise require an exponential number of measurements.

Having defined the setup of quantum state certification, the
main question we aim to answer is determining the fewest
number of copies of the state ρ needed to accurately assess
whether the fidelity ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ is close to one. We introduce a
new approach to solve this problem by defining the concept of
shadow overlap. We demonstrate that shadow overlap can be
estimated using simple single-qubit measurements performed
on the lab state ρ and a few queries to the target state’s
amplitudes. This method enables the certification of almost all
quantum states with a few single-qubit measurements. These
single-qubit measurements are feasible on many experimental
platforms and typically generate data that is computationally
simpler to process. At first glance, it may seem counterintuitive
that single-qubit measurements could certify highly entangled
states, given the property of local indistinguishability—where
two entangled states can be perfectly distinguishable globally but appear identical when examining individual qubits.
However, we show that this intuition is misleading and that
the post-measurement single-qubit states of a highly entangled
system can, in fact, be effectively used for state certification.

Abstract—A fundamental challenge in quantum information
science is certifying that an n-qubit state ρ prepared in the
lab closely matches a target state |ψ⟩. Previous approaches to
this problem often require deep quantum circuits, exponentially
many single-qubit measurements, or are limited to specific state
families. In this work, we introduce a new method that leverages
a connection between state certification and the mixing time of a
random walk, allowing almost all n-qubit target states, including
those with exponential circuit complexity, to be certified with
only O(n2 ) single-qubit measurements. Our protocol is broadly
compatible with various experimental platforms and has applications in benchmarking quantum systems, optimizing quantum
circuits, and efficiently learning and verifying representations of
quantum states—such as neural networks and tensor networks—
using only single-qubit measurements. Moreover, these verified
representations enable the efficient prediction of highly non-local
properties of ρ that would otherwise require an exponential
number of measurements.
Index Terms—Quantum computing, Machine learning, Complexity theory

I. I NTRODUCTION
A central problem in many scientific studies of quantum
physics is determining whether the quantum state of a system
matches a theoretical prediction or a desired model. This can
be addressed through a quantum state certification procedure,
which verifies if an arbitrary n-qubit state ρ is close to a target
state |ψ⟩, even when |ψ⟩ is highly entangled. We assume that
we can perform measurements on copies of the lab state ρ.
We also assume that the target state |ψ⟩ is defined by a query
model Ψ over an orthonormal basis {|x⟩ | x ∈ {0, 1}n } for
the n qubits, where Ψ returns the complex amplitude ⟨x|ψ⟩ for
any input x ∈ {0, 1}n , up to an overall normalization factor.
The query model of quantum states with a limited number of
qubits can be fully stored in classical memory. Additionally,
many (even highly entangled) quantum states, such as phase
states, coherent Gibbs states, GHZ states, and W states admit
a succinct representation using query models. Beyond these
cases and for larger systems, efficient query access to the
amplitudes of a state can be provided by advanced models
like neural network quantum states or tensor networks, which

II. PAST WORKS
Many past works have studied the problem of certifying the
fidelity ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ between a quantum state |ψ⟩ and a general
state ρ. The full-blown tomography of a 2n -dimensional
quantum state ρ is known to require Θ(4n /ϵ2 ) many copies to
achieve an ϵ error in trace distance—or Θ(4n /ϵ) copies for an
ϵ error measured by infidelity [12]–[14]. While this is, in principle, sufficient for estimating the fidelity ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩, it is also
known that the same certification task can be achieved with a
dramatically lower copy complexity of Θ(1/ϵ2 ), independent
of the system dimensions. Achieving this scaling, however,
entails performing certain quantum operations that are often
contrary to the objective of certification. This includes starting
from the description of a (potentially highly-entangled) nqubit state |ψ⟩ and performing the two-outcome measurement
{|ψ⟩⟨ψ|, 1 − |ψ⟩⟨ψ|}) or preparing independent copies of the

state |ψ⟩ (e.g., to perform the swap test) [15]. The recent
framework of classical shadows [16] improves this by performing Clifford measurements on independent copies of the state
ρ. Implementing randomized Clifford measurements, however,
requires deep circuits that may be practically infeasible. The
efficiency of this protocol further depends on computing the
overlap between the state |ψ⟩ and random stabilizer states,
which for instance, may not be achievable for states with high
stabilizer rank.
Provided that single-qubit Pauli measurements can be performed on the copies of the state ρ, a method known as
the direct fidelity estimation introduced and analyzed in [17]
(also see [18], [19]) can estimate the overlap ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ up to
an additive error ϵ using O(2n /ϵ4 ) number of copies. This
scaling is an O(2n ) improvement on a naive application of the
full tomography scheme but still grows exponentially Ω(2n )
with the number of qubits. A variant of classical shadows can
also be applied by employing randomized Pauli measurements,
where the number of samples required scales exponentially
with the weight of the measured observable. This approach
enables us to effectively investigate only small subsystems
[16] but cannot estimate fidelity with a highly-entangled state
efficiently.
When the target state comes from certain special classes of
states, such as stabilizer states or states generated by shallow
quantum circuits, direct fidelity estimation [17] and classical
shadow based on randomized Pauli measurements [16], [20]
can efficiently certify the target states. Other examples include
hypergraph states [21], output states of IQP circuits [22],
bosonic Gaussian states [19], and fermionic Gaussian states
[23]. For generic random target states, cross entropy benchmarking (XEB) provides a good estimate for fidelity under
certain noise models as studied in [24]–[27].
Finally, extending beyond pure target states, a series of past
works have extensively explored the certification of mixed
states [28]–[30].

Each round of single-qubit measurements in the shadow
overlap protocol in Theorem 1 involves 2 queries to the
amplitudes of the target state |ψ⟩. Therefore, provided that we
have efficient query access to |ψ⟩ and T ≤ poly(n), estimating
the shadow overlap is computationally efficient as well.
While not every quantum state in a given basis has a
polynomial relaxation time, the next theorem shows that for
almost all n-qubit pure states, including those with high entanglement and exponential circuit complexity, the relaxation
time τ is bounded by τ ≤ τ ∗ = O(n2 ). This result implies
that such states can be certified with only a few single-qubit
measurements.
Theorem 2 (Certification of almost all quantum states, informal). For all except an exponentially small 2−Ω(n) fraction
of n-qubit target pure states |ψ⟩, there is a certification procedure that performs single-qubit measurements on O(n2 /ϵ)
samples of an unknown state ρ and, with high probability,
outputs FAILED if the fidelity is low ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ < 1 − ϵ and
outputs C ERTIFIED if the fidelity is high ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ ≥ 1 − 2τϵ ∗ ,
where τ ∗ = O(n2 ).
Beyond random quantum states, we also establish a polynomial bound τ ≤ poly(n) for various structured states, such as
quantum phase states and GHZ-like states with τ = O(n), and
states where |⟨x|ψ⟩|2 matches the ground state distribution of
a gapped, sign-free κ-local Hamiltonian, with τ = O(nκ ).
Even though exhibiting fast mixing can be considered an
assumption concerning the target state, we also present a
scheme that could be used to enforce this assumption by
modifying a given query model Ψ of a target state |ψ⟩. This
scheme runs efficiently and has the following feature: If the
model Ψ satisfies a sufficient condition for fast mixing, known
as the local escape property, then it remains unchanged by the
enforcement procedure. If not, a new model Ψ′ is induced
which satisfies the local escape property and exhibits fast
mixing. However, this comes with the potential cost of Ψ′
being very different from the original model Ψ. We show
that local escape property holds for almost all quantum states,
which is the essential ingredient in our proof of Theorem 2.
We defer the proof of these results and Theorem 1 and
Theorem 2 to the full version of this paper [31].

III. M AIN RESULTS
We present a simple method to certify the overlap ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩
between a target pure state |ψ⟩ and a possibly mixed n-qubit
state ρ. This is accomplished by performing single-qubit Pauli
measurements on each qubit of ρ, yielding an estimate ω̂. The
expectation value E[ω̂], known as the shadow overlap, directly
relates to the fidelity ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ as follows:
E[ω̂] ≥ 1 − ϵ implies ⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ ≥ 1 − τ ϵ,
⟨ψ|ρ|ψ⟩ ≥ 1 − ϵ implies E[ω̂] ≥ 1 − ϵ.

We note that the notion of relaxation time used in our
framework is basis-dependent. In fact, a quantum state can
mix slowly in one basis and mix rapidly in a locally rotated
basis. The GHZ state provides an example of such a state. In
the standard Z-basis, we have |GHZ⟩ = √12 (|0⟩⊗n + |1⟩⊗n ).
Hence the distribution of this state is supported on two vertices
0n and 1n and does not mix under the walk defined by the
transition matrix P (x, y). In the Hadamard
P basis, this state can
be expanded as H ⊗n |GHZ⟩ = √21n−1 x∈even |x⟩ and enjoys
fast mixing, though for this purpose we need to change the
protocol so that the observable L corresponds to a walk that

VI. A PPLICATIONS
This certification procedure has much broader applications
that we also investigate in our complete manuscript [31].
ML tomography of quantum states: We show that the
shadow overlap offers a theoretically sound and practically
feasible approach for learning a machine learning model of a
quantum state or certifying the fidelity of an existing model.
Unlike traditional neural network tomography methods, which
often lack rigorous guarantees and can produce spurious properties, our protocol enables efficient training and certification
of models for large quantum systems, ensuring the accuracy
of neural network predictions.
Efficient estimation of highly-nonlocal observables: A
learned and certified model of a quantum state obtained by
applying our procedure can be used to compute a wide range
of properties of the state that correspond to the expectation
values of sparse observables ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩. Without a verified
model, estimating non-linear observables like the subsystem
purity Tr(ρ2A ) requires an exponentially large number of
samples relative to the size of the subsystem A [16], [34]. In
contrast, our verified quantum state models achieve a sample
complexity of O( ϵ12 ), independent of the subsystem size.
Near-term benchmarking of quantum devices: Our certification procedure provides a flexible and robust method
for benchmarking noisy quantum devices with limited measurements and gate controls. It delivers results that closely
mirror fidelity and outperforms existing approaches, such as
cross-entropy benchmarking (XEB), especially for challenging
families of quantum states where traditional methods often fail.
Optimizing quantum circuits for state preparation: We
also demonstrate that the shadow overlap has advantageous
properties for training quantum circuits. Unlike fidelity-based
approaches, which are prone to the barren plateau phenomenon
[35], [36], the shadow overlap behaves similarly to the Hamming distance when the target state’s amplitudes are distributed
across the hypercube {0, 1}n and lacks global correlations.
This allows the shadow overlap to improve gradually with each
step in the state preparation process, whereas fidelity typically
remains close to zero until the circuit reaches a sufficient
size, after which it increases abruptly. Consequently, shadow
overlap can be more effective than fidelity for optimizing
quantum circuits in certain scenarios.
